title: Python Fundamentals & Setup
description: Complete introduction to Python programming, from understanding what Python is to setting up your development environment

lessons.title: What is Python?
lessons.description: Discover Python's history, philosophy, and what makes it popular

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what Python is, who created it, and why it's easy to read.

sections.title: 🐍 Python is...
sections.content:
Python is a popular programming language, created by Guido van Rossum in 1991.

It is used for:

• Web development (server-side)
• Software development
• Data analysis and machine learning
• Automating repetitive tasks
• General-purpose programming

```python
print("Hello, World!")
```

That's a complete Python program — one line, no semicolons, no extra setup.

sections.title: ✅ Why Python?
sections.content:
• Works on many platforms (Windows, Mac, Linux, Raspberry Pi)
• Simple, English-like syntax that's quick to learn
• Fewer lines of code than many other languages
• Runs on an interpreter, so code executes as soon as it's written
• Supports procedural, object-oriented, and functional styles

sections.title: 📌 Good to Know
sections.content: The newest major version is Python 3, which this course uses throughout. Python 2 is no longer supported (its end-of-life was 2020), so all new code should target Python 3.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Following an old tutorial written for Python 2 — syntax like `print "hi"` (no parentheses) will not run in Python 3.

questions.question: Who created Python?
questions.explanation: Guido van Rossum created Python and released it in 1991.

questions.question: Which version of Python should new projects use?
questions.explanation: Python 2 reached end-of-life in 2020; all new work should use Python 3.

questions.question: What does `print("Hello, World!")` do?
options: Displays the text Hello, World! on the screen
questions.explanation: print() outputs text to the console.

questions.question: Is Python's syntax closer to plain English or symbolic math notation?
questions.explanation: Readability is one of Python's core design goals.

questions.question: Python runs on...
questions.explanation: Python is cross-platform.

questions.question: What kind of language is Python (execution-wise)?
questions.explanation: Python code is executed by an interpreter, line by line.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a common Python use case?
options: Low-level device firmware requiring microsecond timing
questions.explanation: Python is generally not chosen for hard real-time firmware work.

questions.question: What happens if you run Python 2 style `print "hi"` in Python 3?
questions.explanation: Python 3 requires print to be called as a function: print("hi").

exercise.prompt:

exercise.tests: # Check that the program runs successfully

lessons.title: Python Syntax & print()
lessons.description: Learn Python's core syntax rules: indentation, comments, and output

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write correctly indented code, add comments, and print output.

sections.title: 📐 Indentation Matters
sections.content:
Unlike many languages, Python uses indentation (whitespace) to define code blocks — there are no curly braces.

```python
if 5 > 2:
    print("Five is greater than two!")
```

The indented line belongs to the `if` statement. Consistent indentation (usually 4 spaces) is required, or Python raises an `IndentationError`.

sections.title: 💬 Comments
sections.content:
Comments start with `#` and are ignored when the code runs — useful for explaining *why*, not just *what*.

```python
# This is a comment
print("Hello")  # This runs; the comment doesn't
```

sections.title: 🖨️ print() Basics
sections.content:
```python
print("Hello")
print("Hello", "World")     # multiple values
print(1 + 2)                # 3
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Inconsistent indentation (mixing tabs and spaces) is one of the most common beginner errors in Python.

questions.question: How does Python define a block of code?
questions.explanation: Indentation level shows which lines belong together.

questions.question: What symbol starts a comment in Python?
questions.explanation: The hash symbol marks the rest of the line as a comment.

questions.question: What happens with inconsistent indentation?
questions.explanation: Python requires consistent whitespace to define blocks correctly.

questions.question: What does `print(1 + 2)` output?
questions.explanation: print() evaluates the expression first, then displays the result.

questions.question: Are comments executed when the program runs?
questions.explanation: Comments exist purely for human readers.

questions.question: What's the conventional indentation size in Python?
questions.explanation: PEP 8 recommends 4 spaces per indentation level.

questions.question: Does Python require semicolons at the end of each line?
questions.explanation: Line breaks alone separate statements in Python.

questions.question: What does `print("a", "b")` output?
questions.explanation: print() joins multiple arguments with a space by default.

lessons.title: Installing Python & Choosing an Editor
lessons.description: Set up Python on your computer and pick an editor to write code in

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Install Python from python.org, verify the install, and pick a starter editor.

sections.title: ⬇️ Installing Python
sections.content:
Download the latest Python 3 installer from **python.org/downloads** for your operating system.

**Windows:** Run the installer and check 'Add Python to PATH' before clicking Install.

**macOS:** Python often comes with the OS, but install the latest via `brew install python3` or the python.org installer.

**Linux:** Usually preinstalled; update with your package manager, e.g. `sudo apt install python3`.

sections.title: ✅ Verifying Your Install
sections.content:
```bash
python --version
# or
python3 --version
```
You should see something like `Python 3.12.x`.

sections.title: 🛠️ Choosing an Editor
sections.content:
You can write Python in any text editor, but a code-aware editor helps a lot:

• **VS Code** — free, lightweight, huge community, great for beginners
• **PyCharm** — a full Python-focused IDE
• **Jupyter Notebook** — great for data science and step-by-step experimentation

For this course, VS Code or any editor you're comfortable with works well.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to check 'Add Python to PATH' on Windows, which means typing `python` in a terminal won't be recognized.

questions.question: Where should you download Python from?
questions.explanation: python.org is the official, safe source.

questions.question: What command checks your installed Python version?
questions.explanation: --version (or -V) prints the interpreter's version.

questions.question: Why check 'Add Python to PATH' on Windows?
options: So you can run 'python' from any terminal location
questions.explanation: PATH lets your OS find the python executable from any directory.

questions.question: Which editor is a full dedicated Python IDE?
questions.explanation: PyCharm is built specifically for Python development.

questions.question: What is VS Code known for?
options: Being lightweight, free, and highly customizable
questions.explanation: VS Code is a popular general-purpose, extensible editor.

questions.question: Which tool is especially good for data science exploration?
questions.explanation: Jupyter's interactive cells suit iterative data work.

questions.question: On macOS, which command can install Python 3 via Homebrew?
questions.explanation: Homebrew is a common macOS package manager.

questions.question: What should you do after installing Python?
questions.explanation: Verifying confirms the installation succeeded correctly.

lessons.title: Running Your First Python File
lessons.description: Write and execute a .py file from the command line

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Create a .py file, run it from a terminal, and understand the REPL as an alternative.

sections.title: 📝 The 'Hello, World!' File
sections.content:
Create a file called `hello.py` with a text editor:

```python
print("Hello, World!")
```

sections.title: ▶️ Running It
sections.content:
Open a terminal in the same folder and run:

```bash
python hello.py
# or on some systems:
python3 hello.py
```

You should see:
```
Hello, World!
```

sections.title: ⌨️ The Python REPL
sections.content:
You can also run Python interactively without saving a file — great for quick tests.

```bash
python
>>> print("Hello!")
Hello!
>>> 2 + 2
4
>>> exit()
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Running `python hello.py` from the wrong folder, which causes a 'file not found' error — make sure your terminal is in the same directory as the file.

questions.question: What extension do Python script files use?
questions.explanation: The standard extension is .py.

questions.question: How do you run a file called hello.py?
questions.explanation: You pass the filename to the python command.

questions.question: What is the Python REPL used for?
options: Running code interactively, one line at a time
questions.explanation: REPL stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop, perfect for experimentation.

questions.question: How do you exit the Python REPL?
questions.explanation: exit() or the platform-specific shortcut ends the session.

questions.question: What causes a 'file not found' error when running a script?
options: Running the command from the wrong directory
questions.explanation: The terminal needs to be in (or point to) the file's folder.

questions.question: What does typing `2 + 2` directly into the REPL show?
questions.explanation: The REPL evaluates and prints results immediately.

questions.question: Which command might you need instead of `python` on some systems?
questions.explanation: Some systems map 'python' to Python 2 or nothing, requiring python3 explicitly.

questions.question: What's a benefit of saving code in a .py file versus only using the REPL?
options: You can save, reuse, and re-run the same program later
Files run faster than the REPL always
questions.explanation: Scripts are persistent and repeatable, unlike a REPL session.

lessons.title: Python Package Manager: pip
lessons.description: Install and manage third-party packages with pip

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Install, list, and uninstall packages using pip, Python's package manager.

sections.title: 📦 What is pip?
sections.content:
pip is Python's tool for installing packages from **PyPI** (the Python Package Index) — a repository of thousands of reusable libraries.

```bash
pip install requests
```

This downloads and installs the `requests` package so you can `import requests` in your code.

sections.title: 🔧 Common pip Commands
sections.content:
```bash
pip install package_name        # install
pip install package_name==1.2.0 # install a specific version
pip list                        # show installed packages
pip show package_name           # show details about one package
pip uninstall package_name      # remove a package
pip install --upgrade pip       # upgrade pip itself
```

sections.title: 🔒 A Note on Virtual Environments
sections.content: In real projects, it's best practice to install packages inside a virtual environment (`python -m venv myenv`) rather than globally, so each project's dependencies stay isolated. This is covered in more depth in a later module.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Installing packages globally for every project, which can cause version conflicts between projects that need different versions of the same package.

questions.question: What does pip stand for/manage?
questions.explanation: pip installs and manages third-party Python packages.

questions.question: Where do pip packages typically come from?
questions.explanation: PyPI is pip's default source.

questions.question: What command installs the 'requests' package?
questions.explanation: install is the pip subcommand for adding new packages.

questions.question: How do you see all currently installed packages?
questions.explanation: list displays every installed package and its version.

questions.question: How do you remove a package?
questions.explanation: uninstall is the correct subcommand.

questions.question: Why use virtual environments alongside pip?
options: To isolate each project's dependencies and avoid conflicts
They're required by pip to function
They replace the need for Python
questions.explanation: Isolation prevents one project's packages from clashing with another's.

questions.question: How do you install a specific version of a package?
questions.explanation: == pins the exact version to install.

questions.question: What does `pip install --upgrade pip` do?
options: Updates pip itself to the latest version
questions.explanation: This upgrades the pip tool, not your project's packages.

exercise.title: Install Your First Package
exercise.prompt:
Open your terminal and install the requests package:

pip install requests

Then check whether it was installed:

pip show requests
exercise.challenge:
Run:

pip list

Can you find the requests package in the list?
exercise.hint: Type the commands in your terminal one at a time. pip show requests should display details about the package if the install worked.
